title: Our 1-minute crypto backtest looked profitable until we included trading costs
author: BlackGreep
selftext:
I've been working on a local trading strategy research project for a while, and we recently finished our first proper historical backtest using BTC, ETH and SOL 1-minute data from November 1–7, 2025.

We tested a regime-adaptive trend pullback strategy with a $10,000 starting balance, 5x leverage and 1% risk per trade. The engine uses next-open execution, position sizing, trading fees and modeled slippage.

The interesting part was the result. We ended up with 13 closed trades, 3 winners and 10 losers. Before costs, the strategy made $76.80. Trading fees came to $251.10, and modeled slippage added another $83.70 in costs. The final result was a loss of $258.01.

We also checked all 13 trades independently against the execution prices, position sizes, fees and equity calculations. Everything reconciled, so at least we know where the losses came from.

It's still a small sample, and some margin and liquidation assumptions are provisional. I'm not claiming the strategy is profitable or that one week proves anything.

Next we're working on reproducibility, out-of-sample testing and improving how the results are explained.

I'm curious how others approach this. When a short-timeframe strategy looks decent before costs but falls apart afterward, do you usually try to improve execution, reduce trading frequency, or consider the underlying edge too weak?

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
13 trades in one week can't tell you if the edge is weak, the gross number is noise at that size too. before touching execution I'd run the same rules over many months and a few different regimes, and look at gross profit per trade there.  
then compare it to your real cost per round trip. if the gross edge per trade is clearly bigger than the costs, work on execution. if it's about the same size, fewer and longer trades is the usual fix. if it's smaller, the edge is too weak and no execution trick saves it. and keep in mind that with 5x leverage, fees grow with notional, not with risk, so they hit harder than the 1% risk suggests.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
That's a fair point. I agree that 13 trades over one week aren't nearly enough to judge whether the strategy has a real edge.

What caught my attention was how much the costs outweighed the gross result in this particular sample. We're planning to test the same rules across longer periods and different market conditions before drawing conclusions.

Your point about leverage and fees being based on notional exposure rather than the 1% risk is especially important. I think comparing gross profit per trade against actual round-trip costs will be a useful next step.

Appreciate the detailed feedback.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body: one tip before you extend it: freeze the rules exactly as they are now and don't tweak them after seeing the longer run. otherwise the bigger sample just becomes a bigger place to fit. curious what it shows, post it when you have it.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
That's exactly the plan. The strategy rules are already versioned and fingerprinted, so we can keep the original configuration unchanged for the longer tests.

I don't want to optimize it based on what we see afterward and then pretend the results are independent.

The next step is checking reproducibility and running the frozen rules on separate data. I'll share what we find, even if the results are worse.

comments.author: zulfi001
comments.body:
your costs are 4x your gross profit so i don’t think better execution saves this. each trade made around $6 and paid around $26 in fees and slippage, the edge is just too thin for 1 min  
my first version lost money too once i bumped fees up. fewer longer trades helped way more than any execution stuff. also 13 trades in a week is way too small to tell anything imo, i’d run it over a few months first

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Yeah, the difference between roughly $6 gross per trade and $26 in costs is pretty hard to ignore.

I agree that optimizing execution alone probably won't solve much if that relationship holds over a larger sample.

For now, I want to keep the strategy rules exactly as they are and test them over longer periods and different market conditions before making changes.

Your experience with fewer, longer trades is interesting though. That's something worth investigating separately after we establish a proper baseline. Appreciate the feedback.

comments.author: grahamhart_
comments.body: Don’t send them anything. A legit exchange shouldn’t demand prepaid “taxes” to unlock selling or withdrawals; that screams advance-fee scam. I’ve used changenow for swaps without that nonsense, but always verify the real domain and keep transaction records.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: same lesson as your SOL runs last month, just louder at 1-minute: the edge per trade has to clear a round trip, and at that bar size it rarely does. one week from early November is also one mood of the market, so even the after-cost number is a sample of about one.

comments.author: PointDexter6508
comments.body:
Props for reconciling every trade. Most people never get that far.
The real takeaway is that your gross edge was about $77 per week while costs ran $335. At that ratio, it's a question of how many trades you take, not whether the signal works. Fewer trades with a larger expected move each would change the math fast.
Also, 13 trades is too small to say anything about the edge itself, so treat this as proof the pipeline works.

replies.author: Zealou-sidealIron
replies.body: Rare to see someone share the unflattering numbers. Respect

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body: Appreciate it. I think sharing the losing results is just as important as sharing the winning ones. Sometimes you learn more from figuring out why something failed.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
That's pretty much how I'm looking at it too. The first goal was to make sure the engine could produce results we could actually verify, rather than just a nice-looking equity curve.

The cost difference was bigger than I expected, but I agree that 13 trades aren't enough to judge the strategy itself.

I'm planning to keep the original rules unchanged and test them over a longer period first. After that, exploring fewer trades with larger expected moves could be interesting as a separate version.

Appreciate the feedback.
